prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) relies on static datasets that often aggregate data from diverse sources, such as varying human demonstrations, different exploration strategies, or multiple distinct policies. This aggregation creates a fundamental challenge: **multi-modal action distributions**. In many states, there may be multiple valid but conflicting actions (e.g., driving left or right to avoid an obstacle).

Current offline RL methods typically assume the behavior policy follows a unimodal distribution (e.g., a single Gaussian). When trained on multi-modal data, these methods often converge to the mean of the distribution. In scenarios with conflicting valid actions, the "average" action is frequently invalid or dangerous (e.g., driving straight into the obstacle). While recent approaches utilize complex generative models (GANs, Diffusion) to model the full distribution, these add significant computational complexity and often model suboptimal modes that are irrelevant for the final task. We need a method that can handle multi-modality without collapsing into invalid averages, while avoiding the overhead of modeling every possible behavior in the dataset.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that to achieve optimal performance in multi-modal offline RL, it is unnecessary to model the entire distribution of behavior. Instead, **learning from a single, locally optimal mode** is sufficient.

Our intuition is that if we can decompose the behavior policy into distinct modes (clusters of actions) and evaluate the expected return of each mode independently, we can identify the "best" mode for any given state. By filtering out suboptimal modes and performing imitation learning *only* on the highest-value mode, we can train a simple unimodal policy that avoids the pitfalls of action averaging while maximizing returns.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a "Learning on One Mode" (LOM) framework. This approach will operate in a three-step pipeline designed to distill complex dataset behaviors into a streamlined optimal policy.

1.  **Multi-Modal Behavior Modeling (The Decomposition Phase):**
    We will first model the underlying behavior policy of the dataset using a Mixture Density Network (MDN) to output a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). Unlike standard behavioral cloning which seeks a single mean, this module will learn to output multiple distinct Gaussian components (modes) and their mixing coefficients for every state. This effectively separates conflicting behaviors into discrete options.

2.  **Hyper-Policy and Hyper Q-Function (The Evaluation Phase):**
    We introduce the concept of a "Hyper-MDP." In this abstraction, the agent's decision is not just which raw action to take, but which *mode index* to select.
    *   We will design a **Hyper Q-function** that takes a state and a *mode index* as input.
    *   This function will estimate the expected return of selecting a specific mode and following the policy associated with that mode thereafter.
    *   This allows us to evaluate the quality of different behavioral clusters (e.g., "aggressive driving mode" vs. "conservative driving mode") at any given state.

3.  **Greedy Mode Selection and Weighted Imitation:**
    Using the Hyper Q-function, we will derive a **Greedy Hyper-Policy** that dynamically selects the mode index with the highest expected return for the current state.
    *   Once the optimal mode is identified, we will perform weighted imitation learning targeted specifically at the actions belonging to that mode.
    *   The final learned policy will be a simple unimodal distribution that mimics the best mode of the behavior policy. This filters out noise and suboptimal trajectories found in the original dataset.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Framework:** We aim to formalize the "Hyper-MDP," providing a theoretical basis for mode selection as a distinct decision-making layer in RL.
*   **Robustness to Multi-modality:** This approach will solve the "averaging" problem inherent in unimodal assumptions, preventing the generation of out-of-distribution or invalid actions in complex environments.
*   **Simplicity and Efficiency:** Unlike diffusion-based or GAN-based approaches that carry heavy inference costs to model the full distribution, our method yields a final policy that is simple (unimodal) and efficient to sample from, while still capturing the benefits of multi-modal data analysis.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We evaluated a novel offline reinforcement learning method, Weighted Imitation Learning on One Mode (LOM), designed to handle multi-modal action distributions. We compared this method against various state-of-the-art baselines across standard benchmarks and custom multi-modal environments.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **D4RL Benchmarks (MuJoCo):** We utilized the `halfcheetah`, `hopper`, and `walker2d` environments. For each environment, we used five dataset types:
        1.  `medium`: 1 million samples from a policy with approx. 1/3 expert performance.
        2.  `medium-replay`: Replay buffer of the medium agent (0.2M-0.4M samples).
        3.  `medium-expert`: A 50-50 split of medium and expert data (<2M samples).
        4.  `expert`: 1 million samples from a fully trained SAC policy.
        5.  `full-replay`: 1 million samples from the final replay buffer of an expert policy.
    *   **Custom Multi-Modal Tasks:** We constructed three tasks using the Fetch robot (FetchReach, FetchPush, FetchPickAndPlace). Datasets contained $4 \times 10^6$ transitions collected by an expert policy. These datasets were designed to be highly multi-modal (e.g., in FetchReach, the robot must reach one of four goals, creating conflicting trajectories in the dataset).

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Normalized Score:** Performance was scaled where 0 represents a random policy and 100 represents an expert policy.
    *   **Success Rate / Reward:** For Fetch tasks, rewards were structured based on reaching specific quadrants (Reward of 2 for first quadrant, 1 for others).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Standard Offline RL:** OneStep, AWAC, CQL, TD3BC.
    *   **Multi-Modal Specific:** LAPO, DMPO, WCGAN (Weighted Conditioned GAN), WCVAE (Weighted Conditioned VAE).
    *   **Simple Baselines (for Fetch tasks):** Behavior Cloning (BC) using a unimodal Gaussian, Mixture Density Network (MDN) using a GMM policy.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Hardware/Code:** Experiments were run over 4 random seeds.
    *   **Behavior Policy Modelling:** Modeled using a Mixture Density Network (MDN) producing parameters for a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM).
    *   **Hyperparameters:**
        *   Advantage weights ($\beta$): 5
        *   Weight clips ($C$): 50
        *   Polyak averaging coefficient: 0.995
        *   Target update delay: 2
        *   Number of Gaussian components ($M$): Varied between $\{2, 5, 10, 15, 20\}$; specific analysis performed on sensitivity to $M$.
    *   **Network Architecture:**
        *   GMM Policy: `[state_dim, 512, 512, 2 * ac_dim + M]`
        *   Learned Policy: `[state_dim, 512, 512, ac_dim]`
        *   Q-network: `[state_dim + ac_dim, 512, 512, 1]`
        *   Hyper Q-function: `[state_dim + M, 512, 512, M]`

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Performance vs. Baselines (General)**
*   In the D4RL benchmark study, our method (LOM) achieved the highest mean score in 12 out of 15 evaluated tasks.
*   Specifically, on highly multi-modal datasets (medium-replay and full-replay), LOM consistently surpassed all baseline methods.
*   In the custom Fetch robotics tasks, LOM outperformed baseline algorithms by an average of 53%.

**Action Distribution Analysis (FetchReach)**
*   We visualized the action distributions learned by different methods in the FetchReach task, where the dataset contained conflicting actions toward four different goals.
*   **Behavior Cloning (BC):** Learned an averaged action distribution centered in the middle of the four targets, failing to reach any specific goal effectively.
*   **MDN:** Successfully reconstructed the multi-modal distribution, showing four distinct clusters corresponding to the four goals.
*   **AWAC:** Learned to prioritize the optimal quadrant (top right) but generated a wide distribution that leaked into Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) regions.
*   **LOM:** Successfully identified the single optimal mode (top right quadrant) and learned a focused distribution within that mode, filtering out suboptimal actions.

**Ablation Study: Number of Gaussian Components ($M$)**
*   We analyzed the effect of varying the number of mixture components $M$ in the Gaussian Mixture Model (values tested: 1, 5, 10, 15, 20).
*   **Medium-Replay Datasets:** Performance generally improved monotonically as $M$ increased from 1 to 20.
*   **Full-Replay Datasets:** Performance gains were observed up to $M=10$, after which performance plateaued or slightly diminished.
*   **Visualization of $M$:**
    *   **Small $M$ (e.g., 2):** Resulted in modes with large standard deviations, causing the policy to capture actions outside the dataset (OOD).
    *   **Large $M$ (e.g., 20, 50):** Resulted in modes with extremely small standard deviations. The imitated actions collapsed to single points, leading to overly narrow learning domains.
    *   **Conclusion:** A moderate value of $M$ balances coverage and precision; $M$ primarily influences the domain of imitated actions.

**Toy Example Analysis (1-Step MDP / Double Circle)**
*   We compared modeling capabilities on a 1-step MDP with a "Double Circle" action distribution.
*   **Gaussian:** Failed to separate modes, covering the center area (invalid actions).
*   **CVAE & CGAN:** Demonstrated better mode separation than Gaussian but still showed some indistinct boundaries.
*   **MDN:** Showed the clearest boundaries between modes with minimal overlap.
*   **Reward-Weighted Learning:** When learning from the top-ranked MDN components (LOM approach), the resulting distribution closely adhered to the in-distribution, high-reward regions (first and third quadrants) better than weighted Gaussian, weighted CVAE, or weighted CGAN.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures


## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Offline reinforcement learning (RL) relies on static datasets collected by behavior policies to learn optimal control strategies. A critical and often overlooked challenge in this domain is the multi-modality of action distributions in real-world heterogeneous datasets. Such datasets often aggregate experiences from diverse sources—multiple policies, human demonstrations, or distinct exploration strategies—resulting in states where multiple valid, yet conflicting, actions exist (e.g., navigating left or right around an obstacle).

Most existing offline RL methods implicitly assume a unimodal Gaussian action distribution. When applied to multi-modal data, this assumption forces the learned policy to converge toward an average action (e.g., going straight into the obstacle), which is often suboptimal or invalid. While recent approaches utilize expressive generative models like GANs, VAEs, or diffusion models to capture the full distribution, these methods introduce significant computational complexity and often model the entire distribution—including suboptimal modes—rather than focusing on the optimal strategy. We identify a need for a framework that can explicitly disentangle these modes and selectively learn only from the most advantageous one.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **Weighted Imitation Learning on One Mode (LOM)**. Our central hypothesis is that in multi-modal offline RL, it is unnecessary to model the full action distribution. Instead, sufficient and superior performance can be achieved by:
1.  Decomposing the behavior policy into distinct Gaussian modes.
2.  Evaluating the expected return of each distinct mode dynamically.
3.  Imitating only the single, highest-value mode for any given state.

By introducing a "Hyper-Markov Decision Process," we hypothesize we can treat the selection of an action mode as a high-level decision (hyper-action), allowing us to derive a greedy hyper-policy that selects the optimal mode before performing fine-grained action selection. This should prevent mode-averaging and reduce the risk of out-of-distribution (OOD) actions.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will construct a three-stage framework: (1) Multi-modal behavior modeling via Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM), (2) Hyper-policy evaluation and selection, and (3) Weighted imitation learning on the selected mode.

### 1. Multi-Modal Behaviour Policy Modelling
We will model the behavior policy $\pi_b(a|s)$ using a Mixture Density Network (MDN) to parameterize a GMM. This allows us to capture diverse clusters of actions associated with a state. The policy will be expressed as:

$$ \pi_b(a|s) = \sum_{i=1}^{M} \alpha^i(s) \phi^i(a|s) $$

Here:
*   $M$ is the number of Gaussian components (modes).
*   $\alpha^i(s)$ represents the mixing coefficient for mode $i$ at state $s$, modeled via a softmax output.
*   $\phi^i(a|s)$ is the Gaussian component for mode $i$, defined by mean $\mu_i(s)$ and standard deviation $\sigma_i(s)$.

We will learn the parameters $\rho$ of this network by minimizing the negative log-likelihood over the dataset $\mathcal{D}$:
$$ \mathcal{L}(\rho) = - \mathbb{E}_{(s, a) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \log \pi_\rho(a \mid s) \right] $$

### 2. The Hyper-Markov Decision Process (H-MDP) and Hyper Q-Function
We formalize the mode selection problem by defining a Hyper-MDP. We introduce a hyper-action space $\mathcal{A}_H = \{1, \dots, M\}$ which indexes the modes.

**Hyper-Policy:**
We define a hyper-policy $\zeta(u|s)$ which maps states to a probability distribution over the mode indices $u \in \mathcal{A}_H$. The composite policy $\pi_\zeta$ is then:
$$ \pi_\zeta(a|s) = \sum_{u \in \mathcal{A}_H} \zeta(u|s) \phi^u(a|s) $$

**Hyper Q-Function:**
To evaluate the quality of a specific mode, we propose a Hyper Q-function, $\mathcal{Q}_H^\zeta(s, u)$, representing the expected return of selecting mode $u$ at state $s$ and following hyper-policy $\zeta$ thereafter. Crucially, we link this to the standard state-action value function $Q^{\pi}(s, a)$:

$$ \mathcal{Q}_H^\zeta(s, u) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \phi^u(\cdot | s)} \left[ Q^{\pi_\zeta}(s, a) \right] $$

**Implementation:**
We will first learn a standard Q-function $Q_\psi$ parameterised by $\psi$ for the behavior policy via standard TD-error minimization. Subsequently, we will learn the behavioral hyper Q-function $Q_\phi(s, u)$ (parameterized by $\phi$) by minimizing the squared difference between the hyper Q-value and the expected Q-value of actions sampled from the mode:

$$ \mathcal{L}(\phi) = \mathbb{E}_{s_t \sim \mathcal{D}, u \sim \text{Uniform}(\mathcal{A}_H)} \left[ \left( Q_\phi(s_t, u) - \mathbb{E}_{a_t \sim \phi^u(\cdot | s_t)} \left[ Q_\psi(s_t, a_t) \right] \right)^2 \right] $$

### 3. Mode Selection and Greedy Hyper-Policy
Using the learned hyper Q-function, we will define a greedy hyper-policy $\zeta_g$ that deterministically selects the mode with the highest expected return for each state:

$$ \zeta_g(s) = \arg \max_{u \in \mathcal{A}_H} Q_H^{\zeta_b}(s, u) $$

This yields a greedy composite policy $\pi_{\zeta_g}(a|s) = \phi^{\zeta_g(s)}(a|s)$, which is a unimodal Gaussian distribution corresponding to the best identified mode.

### 4. Policy Learning via Weighted Imitation
Finally, we will perform weighted imitation learning to optimize the target policy $\pi_\theta$. Instead of imitating the raw dataset, we generate samples from the greedy unimodal policy $\pi_{\zeta_g}$.

We formulate the optimization as maximizing the advantage-weighted log-likelihood. The objective function is:

$$ J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathcal{D}, a \sim \pi_{\zeta_g}(\cdot | s)} \left[ \exp_{\text{clip}} \left( \frac{1}{\beta} A^{\pi_{\zeta_g}}(s, a) \right) \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s) \right] $$

Where:
*   $\beta$ is a temperature hyper-parameter.
*   $A^{\pi_{\zeta_g}}(s, a)$ is the advantage function. We will approximate this using $Q_\psi(s, a) - Q_\psi(s, \bar{a}_t)$, where $\bar{a}_t$ is the mean action of the mode, to reduce computational cost.
*   $\pi_\theta$ is the final policy network we intend to deploy.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Framework for Heterogeneous Data:** We will provide a mathematically rigorous method for handling multi-modal offline RL datasets without the complexity of diffusion models or the mode-collapse of unimodal Gaussian policies.
2.  **Theoretical Guarantees:** We aim to prove that our greedy hyper-policy improves upon the behavior policy ($V^{\pi_{\zeta_g}} \geq V^{\pi_b}$) and that the final LOM policy improves upon the greedy hyper-policy ($V^{\pi_L} \geq V^{\pi_{\zeta_g}}$).
3.  **Algorithmic Efficiency:** By reducing the problem to learning on a single, optimal Gaussian mode, we expect to achieve state-of-the-art performance with inference speeds comparable to standard unimodal policies, avoiding the iterative sampling costs associated with generative approaches.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
